lessons.title: Cell division
lessons.summary: Find out how chromosomes carry genes, how the cell cycle and mitosis make identical new cells, and how stem cells can become any cell type.
objectives: I can describe how chromosomes are arranged in the nucleus of a body cell.
I can describe the three stages of the cell cycle, including mitosis.
I can explain why mitosis is important for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
I can compare embryonic, adult and plant meristem stem cells.
I can evaluate the benefits and risks of using stem cells in medicine.

activities.title: Chromosomes and genes
activities.content:
## Chromosomes

The nucleus of a cell holds the instructions for building and running the organism. Those instructions are written in **DNA**, and the DNA is packaged into long, coiled structures called **chromosomes**.

Each chromosome carries a large number of **genes**. A gene is a short section of DNA that codes for one particular characteristic, such as the pigment in your eyes.

In a normal human body cell the chromosomes come in **pairs** – one of each pair came from the mother's egg and the other from the father's sperm. Humans have **23 pairs**, so **46 chromosomes** in total.

- Body cells with two full sets are described as **diploid**.
- Gametes (sperm and egg cells) have only one set, 23 chromosomes, and are called **haploid**.

The number of chromosomes varies between species: a fruit fly has 8, a dog has 78. What matters for cell division is that every new body cell must receive an *exact copy* of every chromosome.

activities.title: Worked example: counting chromosomes
activities.content:
**A cat has 38 chromosomes in each body cell. How many pairs is that, and how many chromosomes are in a cat's egg cell?**

1. Chromosomes come in pairs, so pairs = 38 ÷ 2 = **19 pairs**.
2. An egg cell carries only one chromosome from each pair, so it has 38 ÷ 2 = **19 chromosomes**.

**When the cat's body cell divides by mitosis, how many chromosomes will each new cell have?**

Mitosis makes copies that are **genetically identical** to the parent cell, so each new cell also has **38** chromosomes.

The pattern to remember: *body cell → mitosis → same number*; *body cell → gametes → half the number*.

question.text: A horse has 64 chromosomes in each body cell. How many chromosomes are in a horse skin cell that has just been produced by mitosis?
question.hint: Mitosis produces cells that are identical to the parent cell.
question.explanation: Mitosis makes genetically identical copies, so the new skin cell also has 64 chromosomes.

activities.title: The cell cycle
activities.content:
## The cell cycle

Body cells go through a repeating series of events called the **cell cycle**. It has three main stages.

**Stage 1 – Growth and DNA replication (interphase).** This is the longest stage. The cell grows larger, makes more ribosomes and mitochondria, and then **copies its DNA** so that every chromosome becomes two identical strands joined together.

**Stage 2 – Mitosis.** The copied chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell. Fibres pull the two copies of each chromosome to opposite ends of the cell. Two new nuclei then form, one at each end.

**Stage 3 – Cytokinesis.** The cytoplasm and cell membrane divide, producing **two cells**. Each new cell is **genetically identical** to the parent and to each other.

```
  one cell --> grow + copy DNA --> mitosis --> two identical cells
      ^                                              |
      |______________________________________________|
```

Mitosis is needed for **growth**, for **repair** of damaged tissue, and in some organisms for **asexual reproduction**. Cells that divide uncontrollably form a **tumour** – this is what happens in cancer.

activities.title: Worked example: describing mitosis
activities.content:
**Question: Describe what happens during mitosis. (3 marks)**

A weak answer just says "the cell splits in two". A strong answer gives the sequence of events in order.

**Model answer:**

1. Before mitosis begins, the DNA has already been copied so each chromosome consists of two identical copies.
2. During mitosis, one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell.
3. The nucleus divides to form two nuclei, and then the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to give two genetically identical cells.

Notice the key vocabulary the examiner is looking for: *chromosomes*, *pulled to each end*, *nucleus divides*, *two identical cells*. Getting the order right is what separates a full-mark answer from a partial one.

question.text: Put the events of the cell cycle in the correct order, starting with the earliest.
question.hint: DNA must be copied before the copies can be separated.
question.explanation: The cell grows and copies its DNA, then the chromosome copies are pulled apart, the nucleus divides and finally the cytoplasm divides.
order: The cell grows and increases the number of ribosomes and mitochondria
The DNA is replicated so each chromosome has two identical copies
The chromosome copies are pulled to opposite ends of the cell
The nucleus divides to form two nuclei
The cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to form two cells

question.text: Which of the following are reasons why multicellular organisms need mitosis? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Think about what a growing child, a healing cut and a strawberry runner have in common.
question.explanation: Mitosis provides new cells for growth, replaces damaged or worn-out cells in repair, and allows some organisms to reproduce asexually. It does not produce gametes; that is a different type of division.

options.feedback: Gametes are made by a different type of division that halves the chromosome number.

activities.title: Stem cells
activities.content:
## Stem cells

Most cells in your body are specialised and can only make more of their own kind. A **stem cell** is different: it is an **undifferentiated** cell that can keep dividing and can develop into many different cell types.

**Embryonic stem cells** come from early-stage embryos. They can differentiate into **any** type of human cell. They are the most flexible, but using them means an embryo is destroyed, which some people object to.

**Adult stem cells** are found in certain tissues, such as **bone marrow**. They can only differentiate into a limited range of cells – bone marrow stem cells form different types of blood cell, for example. They can be taken from a patient with little harm.

**Meristem cells** in plants are found in the tips of roots and shoots. Unlike animal stem cells they keep the ability to form **any** plant cell type throughout the plant's life. This is why a cutting from a stem can grow roots and become a whole new plant.

Stem cells from meristems are used to **clone rare plants** quickly and cheaply, protecting species from extinction, and to produce large numbers of identical crop plants with useful features such as disease resistance.

activities.title: Worked example: choosing a stem cell source
activities.content:
**A patient has a disease that destroys nerve cells in the brain. A doctor considers treating them with stem cells. Which source of stem cells is most suitable, and what is the main drawback?**

- Nerve cells are not blood cells, so **adult stem cells from bone marrow** are unlikely to be able to make them.
- **Embryonic stem cells** can differentiate into any cell type, including nerve cells, so they are the most suitable.
- Drawback: they must be taken from an embryo, which raises **ethical objections**, and the patient's immune system may **reject** the cells because they are not the patient's own.

A possible solution is **therapeutic cloning**: an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient, so the stem cells it provides would not be rejected.

question.text: Complete the sentences about stem cells.

metadata.blanksText: Stem cells are ___ cells that can divide to form many types of cell. In plants, stem cells are found in the ___. In adults, stem cells that form blood cells are found in the bone ___.

question.hint: The first word means 'not yet specialised'. The plant tissue is at root and shoot tips.
question.explanation: Stem cells are undifferentiated. Plant stem cells are found in the meristem. Adult stem cells that make blood cells are in the bone marrow.

activities.title: Stem cells in medicine: benefits and risks
activities.content:
## Weighing up stem cell treatment

Stem cells could be used to treat conditions where cells have been lost or damaged, such as **diabetes** (replacing insulin-producing cells) and **paralysis** (replacing damaged nerve cells).

**Potential benefits**
- Could cure diseases that currently have no cure.
- Therapeutic cloning gives cells with the patient's own genes, so they are **not rejected**.
- Reduces the need for organ donors.

**Risks and objections**
- Stem cells grown in a lab may be **contaminated with viruses** that are passed to the patient.
- Cells that keep dividing could form **tumours**.
- Some people believe an embryo is a potential human life, so destroying it is **unethical** or against their religious beliefs.
- The treatments are new, expensive and their long-term effects are not fully known.

In an evaluation question, give at least one point on each side and then a clear conclusion. Examiners reward balance, not just a list of benefits.

question.text:
Scientists hope to treat a patient with type 1 diabetes by using stem cells to grow new insulin-producing cells.

(a) Explain why embryonic stem cells rather than adult stem cells are more likely to be used for this treatment.

(b) Give **one** medical risk and **one** ethical objection to using embryonic stem cells.
question.hint: Compare what each type of stem cell can turn into. Then think about what can go wrong in the lab and why some people object to the source of the cells.
question.explanation: (a) Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into any type of cell, including insulin-producing cells, whereas adult stem cells can only form a limited range of cell types. (b) Medical risk: viral contamination or tumour formation, or rejection by the immune system. Ethical objection: the embryo is destroyed, and some people regard it as a potential life.

markScheme.criterion: Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into any / all types of cell
Adult stem cells can only form a limited range of cell types (e.g. blood cells)
A medical risk: viral infection/contamination, tumour, rejection
An ethical objection: embryo destroyed / potential life / religious beliefs

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Chromosomes** are made of DNA and carry **genes**. Body cells have chromosomes in **pairs** (23 pairs in humans).
- The **cell cycle**: grow and copy DNA → **mitosis** (chromosome copies pulled apart, nucleus divides) → cytoplasm divides → **two identical cells**.
- Mitosis is needed for **growth, repair and asexual reproduction**.
- **Embryonic** stem cells can form any cell; **adult** stem cells only a few types; plant **meristem** cells can form any plant cell for the whole of the plant's life.
- Stem cell therapy: benefits (treat diabetes, paralysis; therapeutic cloning avoids rejection) versus risks (viral contamination, tumours, ethical objections).

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: the two cells produced by mitosis are genetically identical to each other.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what happens to the DNA before the cell divides.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. The DNA is copied exactly, then one full set goes to each new cell, so both are genetically identical.

practiceQuestions.text: How many chromosomes are there in a normal human body cell?

options.feedback: 23 is the number of pairs, or the number in a gamete.

practiceQuestions.text: During which stage of the cell cycle is the DNA replicated?
practiceQuestions.hint: The copies must exist before they can be separated.
practiceQuestions.explanation: DNA is replicated during the growth stage (interphase) before mitosis begins.

options.feedback: Mitosis separates the copies; they have already been made by then.

options.text: After the two new cells have formed

practiceQuestions.text: Match each type of stem cell to the correct description.
practiceQuestions.hint: One comes from plants, one from early embryos, one from tissues such as bone marrow.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Embryonic stem cells can become any human cell; adult stem cells only a limited range; meristem cells can form any plant cell throughout the plant's life.

pairs.right: Can differentiate into any type of human cell
Can only form a limited range of cell types, such as blood cells
Found in root and shoot tips and can form any plant cell

practiceQuestions.text: A student observes cells under a microscope. Out of 200 cells, 15 are in mitosis. The whole cell cycle takes 24 hours. Estimate how long mitosis lasts, in hours.
practiceQuestions.hint: The fraction of cells in mitosis equals the fraction of the cycle that mitosis takes up.

metadata.blanksText: Cells that divide uncontrollably form a mass of cells called a ___, and this uncontrolled division is the cause of ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: The disease name begins with C.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Uncontrolled cell division forms a tumour, which is the basis of cancer.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain how meristem cells allow a gardener to produce many identical copies of a rare plant.
practiceQuestions.hint: What can meristem cells become, and what will the copies share with the parent?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Meristem cells can differentiate into any type of plant cell, so a small cutting containing meristem can grow into a whole plant. The new plants are clones, genetically identical to the parent.

markScheme.criterion: Meristem cells can differentiate into any type of plant cell / grow into a whole plant
The new plants are clones / genetically identical to the parent

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why stem cells produced by therapeutic cloning are less likely to be rejected by a patient's body than stem cells from an unrelated donor.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about whose genes the cloned cells carry.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In therapeutic cloning the embryo is created using the patient's own genetic material, so the stem cells have the same genes as the patient and the immune system does not recognise them as foreign.

markScheme.criterion: The cells have the same genes / DNA as the patient
So the immune system does not recognise them as foreign / attack them

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following are risks of stem cell treatment? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what could be growing alongside the stem cells in the lab, and what dividing cells can form.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Stem cell cultures may carry viruses, and cells that keep dividing may form tumours. Stem cells do not change a patient's blood group or make chromosomes disappear.

options.text: The cells may be infected with a virus that is passed to the patient
The cells may keep dividing and form a tumour
The patient's blood group will change
The patient's chromosomes will be destroyed

practiceQuestions.text: A cut on the skin heals within a few days. Describe the role of the cell cycle in healing the cut, and explain why the new skin cells are identical to the surrounding cells.
practiceQuestions.hint: Which type of division replaces the lost cells, and what happens to the DNA before division?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cells near the cut go through the cell cycle and divide by mitosis to produce new cells that replace the damaged ones. Before division the DNA is copied exactly, and each new cell gets a full set of chromosomes, so the new cells are genetically identical.

markScheme.criterion: Cells divide by mitosis to replace the damaged / lost cells
The DNA / chromosomes are copied before the cell divides
Each new cell receives a full identical set of chromosomes so they are genetically identical
